title: Codex skills: how to install, write and use them
summary: Install Codex skills, write SKILL.md files, control automatic invocation with openai.yaml, and choose useful skills for code review and engineering tasks.
body_markdown:
Codex skills are folders with a` SKILL.md` file (a name, a description and instructions) that Codex loads when a task matches, plus optional scripts and reference files. You install curated ones with` $skill-installer` , write your own in` .agents/skills` in a repo or` $HOME/.agents/skills` for yourself, and call one by name with` $` or let Codex pick it from its description.


Skills in Codex follow the open[Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/) format, so most of what you write here also runs in other agents. For the format itself and how it compares across tools, see our[guide to agent skills and how SKILL.md works](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/agent-skills) . This guide sticks to Codex: where skills live, how they trigger, how to install and write them, and a short list worth trying. Setup details were checked against official OpenAI documentation on October 15, 2026.


## What a skill is in Codex


OpenAI's Build skills page describes a skill as a directory with a required` SKILL.md` . The file's frontmatter needs` name` and` description` . Everything else is optional:


```text
my  - skill  /
├──   SKILL  . md              # required :    name  ,    description  ,    instructions
├──   scripts  /            #  executable   code
├──   references  /         #  documentation   Codex   reads   when   needed
├──   assets  /             #  templates   and   resources
└──   agents  / openai  . yaml    #  appearance   and   dependency   metadata
```


```text
my  - skill  /
├──   scripts  /            #  executable   code
├──   assets  /             #  templates   and   resources
```


```text
my  - skill  /
├──   scripts  /            #  executable   code
├──   assets  /             #  templates   and   resources
```


The same skills work in ChatGPT and Codex. Codex does not read every skill in full at the start of a session. It first loads each skill's name, description and file path, and reads the full` SKILL.md` only once it picks that skill. OpenAI calls this progressive disclosure.


That initial list has a budget. By default it uses at most 2% of the model's context window, or 8,000 characters when the window size is unknown. You can change it with` skills.max_context_tokens` , up to 10,000 tokens. A large pile of installed skills costs context on every session even when none of them runs, which is one reason to keep descriptions short.


## Where Codex loads skills from


Codex reads skills from these scopes, per OpenAI's docs:


Scope


Location


Use it for


Repo


` $CWD/.agents/skills`


Skills for the folder you started Codex in


Repo


` $CWD/../.agents/skills`


A parent folder, when you're inside a Git repo


Repo


` $REPO_ROOT/.agents/skills`


Skills for the whole repository


User


` $HOME/.agents/skills`


Your personal skills, in every repo


Admin


` /etc/codex/skills`


Machine-wide skills set by an admin


System


Bundled with Codex


Skills OpenAI ships, such as` skill-creator`


A few details from the same page matter in practice:


-


Codex picks up changes to skill files on its own. If an edit doesn't show up, restart Codex.


-


It follows symlinked skill folders, so you can keep skills in one checkout and link them in.


-


If two skills share a` name` , Codex doesn't merge them. Both can show up in the skill selector, so give repo skills distinct names.


Commit repo skills to` .agents/skills` and everyone who opens the repo in Codex gets them. Put personal habits in` $HOME/.agents/skills` .


## How Codex picks a skill


There are two ways a skill runs.


Explicit: in the Codex CLI or the IDE extension, run` /skills` to browse what's loaded, or type` $` followed by the skill name in your prompt, for example` $skill-creator` . In ChatGPT the equivalent is` @` .


Implicit: Codex chooses a skill on its own when your request matches the skill's` description` . The description decides whether that happens. OpenAI's advice is to keep it concise, with a clear scope and the trigger words a user would type. Say when the skill should trigger and when it should not.


Some skills should never run on their own, such as one that pushes code or opens a pull request. Add an` agents/openai.yaml` file with this to keep a skill explicit-only:


```text
policy :
allow_implicit_invocation :    false
```


```text
policy :
allow_implicit_invocation :    false
```


```text
policy :
allow_implicit_invocation :    false
```


The skill still runs when you call it with` $skill-name` . The default is` true` .


To turn a skill off without deleting it, add an entry to` ~/.codex/config.toml` and restart Codex:


```text
[  [  skills  . config  ]  ]
path   =  "/path/to/skill/SKILL.md"
enabled   =  false
```


```text
[  [  skills  . config  ]  ]
path   =  "/path/to/skill/SKILL.md"
enabled   =  false
```


```text

enabled   =  false
```


## How to install Codex skills


### Curated skills with $skill-installer


Codex ships with a system skill called` skill-installer` . Ask for a curated skill by name:


```text
$skill  - installer   gh  - fix  - ci
```


```text
$skill  - installer   gh  - fix  - ci
```


```text
$skill  - installer   gh  - fix  - ci
```


By default it installs from the curated folder of openai/skills. You can also hand it a GitHub folder URL for a skill in the repo's experimental folder or in another repo. The installer's own instructions say it can list what's available and install from other repos, private ones included. Codex detects newly installed skills automatically; restart it if the skill does not appear.


Use the installer for local setup and experiments. For sharing reusable skills with a team, OpenAI recommends packaging them as plugins.


### Install a skill folder manually


Copy a trusted skill's complete folder into` .agents/skills/` in your repository to share it with the team, or` ~/.agents/skills/` for personal use. Keep the directory name consistent with the` name` in its frontmatter:


```text
. agents  / skills  / release  - notes  / SKILL  . md
```


```text
. agents  / skills  / release  - notes  / SKILL  . md
```


```text
. agents  / skills  / release  - notes  / SKILL  . md
```


Keep bundled scripts, references and assets beside the manifest. Check that the skill appears in` /skills` , invoke it with` $release-notes` , and confirm any required tools are installed before relying on it.


### Skills inside plugins


A Codex plugin bundles skills with other pieces, such as MCP servers and hooks. In the Codex CLI, type` /plugins` to open the plugin browser, which groups plugins by marketplace and lets you install or uninstall them. Start a new session after installing before you use a plugin's skills.


You can add other marketplaces from the command line:


```text
codex   plugin   marketplace   add   owner  / repo
codex   plugin   marketplace   list
```


```text
codex   plugin   marketplace   add   owner  / repo
codex   plugin   marketplace   list
```


```text
codex   plugin   marketplace   add   owner  / repo
codex   plugin   marketplace   list
```


A plugin can be nothing more than a wrapper around skills. OpenAI's plugin guide starts with a minimal plugin that packages one skill under a root` skills/` folder, and Codex has a built-in` $plugin-creator` skill that scaffolds one.


### Skills from other repos


Many skill repos on GitHub are written for several agents at once. Read a skill's` SKILL.md` , license and any scripts before installing it: a skill provides instructions your agent follows and code it may run on your machine. Pick skills for tasks you repeat, and check their required tools and expected output before adding more.


## How to write a Codex skill


### Start with $skill-creator


The fastest route is the built-in skill:


```text
$skill  - creator
```


```text
$skill  - creator
```


```text
$skill  - creator
```


It asks what the skill should do and when it should trigger, then drafts the folder. Instruction-only skills are the default. Its own` SKILL.md` gives the main rule for writing one: Codex is already capable, so only add context it doesn't already have.


### Or write SKILL.md by hand


Create a folder whose name matches the skill's` name` , then add` SKILL.md` :


```text
---
name  :    release  - notes
description :    Draft   release   notes   from   merged   PRs   since   the   last   git   tag  .  Use    when   the   user   asks   for    release   notes  ,    a   changelog   entry   or   a   summary   of   what   shipped  .  Do    not   use   for    commit   messages  .
---


1.    Find   the   latest   tag   with    `git describe --tags --abbrev=0`  .
2.    List    merged   PRs   since   that   tag   with    `gh pr list --state merged --search "merged:>=<tag date>"`  .
3.    Group    changes   under   Features  ,    Fixes   and   Internal  .
4.    Output   Markdown  .  Do    not   edit   any   files


```

The Agent Skills[specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) sets the rules both Codex and other agents expect:


Field


Required


Rules


` name`


Yes


Up to 64 characters. Lowercase letters, numbers and hyphens. No leading, trailing or double hyphens. Must match the folder name.


` description`


Yes


Up to 1,024 characters. Says what the skill does and when to use it.


` license`


No


A license name or a bundled license file.


` compatibility`


No


Up to 500 characters on environment needs, such as required packages.


` metadata`


No


String keys and values for anything else.


` allowed-tools`


No


Pre-approved tools. Experimental, and support varies by agent.


The spec also recommends keeping` SKILL.md` under 500 lines and moving detail into` references/` files that the agent loads only when needed.


### Optional: agents/openai.yaml


This file is specific to OpenAI's products. Besides` policy.allow_implicit_invocation` , it supports an` interface` block (display name, short description, icons, brand color and a default prompt, shown in the ChatGPT desktop app) and` dependencies.tools` , where a skill can declare that it needs a tool such as an MCP server:


```text
dependencies :
tools :
-  type  :    "mcp"
value :    "openaiDeveloperDocs"
description :    "OpenAI Docs MCP server"
transport :    "streamable_http"
url :    "https://developers.openai.com/mcp"
```

-  type  :    "mcp"
value :    "openaiDeveloperDocs"

Other agents ignore this file, so it doesn't hurt portability.


### Tips from OpenAI's guide


-


Keep each skill to one job.


-


Prefer instructions over scripts unless you need deterministic behavior or an external tool.


-


Write steps in the imperative, with clear inputs and outputs.


-


Test a few prompts against the description to check the skill triggers when it should, and stays quiet when it shouldn't.

### A review skill before you push


After a skill changes code, inspect the diff and run the relevant checks before committing. Our guide to[reviewing AI-generated code](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/how-to-review-ai-generated-code) covers the failure patterns to check.[Bug Bench's Codex page](https://www.cubic.dev/bugbench/harnesses/codex) tracks bugs in AI-attributed code reviewed by cubic; its observational results reflect both model choice and the work teams assign to each model.


Our product, cubic, publishes skills that run a review inside your agent. To install them for Codex:


```text

```

According to the[skills docs](https://docs.cubic.dev/ide/skills) ,` run-review` reviews uncommitted changes or the current branch through its CLI,` check-pr-comments` handles unresolved PR review feedback, and` cubic-loop` repeats review and fixes up to an iteration limit. In Codex you call them by name or describe the task. For other options, see our post on[a code review skill for Claude Code, Codex and Cursor](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/code-review-skill) .


## Use the same skills in Claude Code and Cursor


Because Codex skills follow the Agent Skills format, the same folder usually works elsewhere. The difference is where each agent looks:


Agent


Project skills


Personal skills


Codex


` .agents/skills/`


` ~/.agents/skills/`


Cursor


` .agents/skills/` or` .cursor/skills/`


` ~/.agents/skills/` or` ~/.cursor/skills/`


Claude Code


` .claude/skills/`


` ~/.claude/skills/`


Cursor's docs say it reads` .agents/skills` and, for compatibility, also` .codex/skills` and` .claude/skills` , so a skill committed for Codex shows up in Cursor without changes. Claude Code's docs list` .claude/skills` and don't mention` .agents/skills` , so for Claude Code you copy or symlink the folder there. Claude Code's docs also note that outside Claude Code only the standard frontmatter fields work, so stick to` name` ,` description` and the other spec fields if you want one skill for every agent. The[Cursor skills guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/cursor-skills) covers Cursor's side, including its own invocation options.


A skill defines a reusable review procedure; Codex also has built-in review commands. Our[Codex code review guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/codex-code-review) explains the local and GitHub review options so you can choose where each check belongs. For setting up Codex itself, start with our[Codex CLI guide](https://www.cubic.dev/blog/codex-cli) .


## FAQ


### Where are Codex skills stored?


OpenAI's docs list` .agents/skills` in the repo (including the current folder, a parent folder inside a Git repo and the repo root),` $HOME/.agents/skills` for personal skills,` /etc/codex/skills` for admin skills, and system skills bundled with Codex. Codex follows symlinks in these folders, so one shared checkout can feed several repos.


### Why isn't Codex using my skill?


Codex chooses skills implicitly by matching your request against each skill's` description` , so a vague description is the usual cause. Rewrite it to name the task and the words a user would type, then test with a few prompts. You can also call it directly with` $skill-name` , check that it appears under` /skills` , and restart Codex if a recent edit hasn't loaded.


### What's the difference between skills and plugins in Codex?


A skill is one folder of instructions and optional scripts. A plugin is a package for distribution that can hold several skills plus MCP servers, browser extensions and hooks, installed through` /plugins` or a marketplace. OpenAI recommends` $skill-installer` and local folders for your own setup and experiments, and plugins for sharing skills with others.


### Are openai/skills and "awesome Codex skills" lists the same thing?


No. openai/skills is OpenAI's own catalog, with system skills bundled into Codex and curated skills you install with` $skill-installer` . "Awesome" lists are community collections on GitHub that link to skills from many authors, so check each one's` SKILL.md` and scripts before installing.


### Can I use Claude skills in Codex?


Usually, yes. Both follow the Agent Skills format, so a folder with a valid` SKILL.md` can move from` .claude/skills` to` .agents/skills` . Fields specific to Claude Code won't do anything in Codex, and the curated` migrate-to-codex` skill exists to move skills, instruction files and MCP config from other tools into Codex.
